question: v04
q: Should I be fixing my home loan right now? What are banks advertising for a 3-year fixed?

transcript.answer:
I can't tell you whether you should fix. That depends on your finances and how much risk you can handle. What I can tell you is what advertised rates are, and fixing currently costs a bit more than variable.

**Advertised owner-occupier rates (RBA indicator rates, September 2026)**

| | Rate |
|---|---|
| **3-year fixed** | **7.02%** |
| Discounted variable (what most borrowers actually get) | 6.80% |
| Standard variable (the headline rate few people pay) | 8.77% |

The 3-year fixed rate has risen quickly. It was as low as 5.52% from August to October 2025, then went up every month or two to 6.74% by mid-2026, and jumped again to 7.02% in September. These are advertised rates. Rates actually paid on new loans are lower: in August 2026 it was about **6.3%** for loans fixed for 3 years or less and **6.2%** for variable (RBA F6). So a good deal should come in well under 7%.

**Why fixed rates are going up**
- **Rate hikes:** The RBA cash rate rose from 3.60% in January 2026 to 4.35% by June. That undid the 2025 cuts. The September average was 4.36%, which may mean a small move right at the end of the month, so check the latest RBA decision.
- **Inflation is still high:** Trimmed mean inflation (the RBA's preferred measure) was **3.6%** in the year to August 2026, and headline inflation was **4.0%**. Both are above the 2–3% target and have been rising, not falling.
- **Bond markets expect more hikes:** The 3-year government bond yield is about **4.91%** (mid-October 2026), up from 3.54% a year earlier. That's well above the 4.35% cash rate, which suggests markets expect the RBA to keep raising rates. Banks set fixed rates from these yields.

**What this means for the decision**
- **The future hikes are already in the price.** A fixed rate of 7.02% against 6.80% variable means you pay about 0.22 percentage points more from day one. Fixing only saves you money if variable rates rise by more than markets already expect, or stay high for longer.
- **You've missed the cheap window.** Fixing at about 5.5% in late 2025 would have been a great result. Now you're paying a price that already assumes rates will keep rising.
- **Fixing is about certainty more than saving money.** If your budget couldn't handle another 0.5–1 percentage point rise, locking in repayments may be worth paying a bit extra. If you could absorb more hikes and want to make extra repayments or use an offset account (usually limited on fixed loans), variable keeps you flexible. Fixed loans also usually charge break fees if you sell or refinance early.
- **You can split the loan.** Fixing part and leaving the rest variable spreads the risk.

**What to do next:** Get actual quotes from your lender and one or two others. What banks actually charge is often 0.5 percentage points or more below these advertised rates. Then work out your repayments under both options, and test the variable option with another 0.5–1 point of hikes. For advice tailored to your situation, a mortgage broker or licensed adviser is the right person to ask.
